description:
We are Schrödinger's Coders, a youth team that is a part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge for the first time! We are a team of three and are doing the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" Challenge. 

No new joiners please.
summary: We developed a simulation of problems that can happen living on the Moon. For example, a mini-asteroid that blows up the outpost. This addresses the challenge as it shows real trade-offs and balances power against oxygen and hull shielding. Rather than overwhelming adolescent players with dozens of complicated stats, the game focuses on three or four real-life essentials needed to stay alive in space, specific to each habitat building. Some include Oxygen, Power (Energy), and Hull Integrity (Structural Health). This is important as regarding flying out to space, and building an outpost, many things can go wrong right under your noses and without prior experience, problems will start to occur without understanding what you need to do. Our Game, "Lunar Dawn," helps build the understanding of these problems without the use of immense and overwhelming stats.
details:
Rather than overwhelming adolescent players with dozens of complicated stats, the game focuses on three or four real-life essentials needed to stay alive in space, specific to each habitat building. They run a lunar outpost, controlling amenities to keep their astronauts safe.

This strategy is beneficial because it lets young players truly understand the difficulties and challenges of running your own outpost that movies and other video games don't show. Each decision to go on a science mission, fix a problem, or request shipments from Earth has a trade-off, like real life, instead of an infinite resource game. The main impact of this simulation games is to allow young learners or learners in general to test hypotheses, make critical mistakes under pressure, and immediately observe cause-and-effect consequences in a zero-risk environment. Experiencing a habitat depressurization or power blackout firsthand builds deeper understanding and maintaining information rather than reading a textbook about closed-loop support.

We used the Unity platform to build our game. One of the reasons that we did this is due to its scalability and outreach potential. We published the game through the web, making it accessible to almost every gamer. We also used Codex (ChatGPT) to write C# scripts, and Gemini and ChatGPT to brainstorm. Our programmer used a laptop to code the game.

Our project is creative as rather than other space based games, our game teaches the importance of understanding the value of understanding real-life systems engineering and off-world survival. Instead of fighting fictional monsters, players confront the genuine, silent enemies of lunar exploration.

Factors our team considered when making this game are the materials needed to build the base, & the lesson it gives players about how much astronauts have to deal with. Rebuilding things such as solar panels and such would not cost much materials and astronauts would regularly recycle broken down equipment for raw metals, but asteroids can cause major damage to lunar outpost leading t astronauts to heavily depend on immediate emergency shipments from Earth. Many factors considered when making the game are the lessons it teaches. Many things like deaths of astronauts has never been done, apart from a a close real-life example from the Soyuz 1 mission (V. Komarov). However, it's never a 0% guarantee as many things can happen reguarding space. So, we included in-game sacrifices and many other things like how to fix solar panels for energy.
